summary: This RFC proposes using TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, to load an operating system or program onto a computer over the network at startup. Machines with no local disk can fetch what they need to boot.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 906 proposes using TFTP, a simple file-transfer protocol, to load a computer's startup code over a network. A machine can request a named file before its normal operating system starts, and can use RARP to learn its network address.

questions: how to boot a computer over tftp
how does a diskless workstation boot over the network
subtitle: A proposal to use TFTP as a common way for a machine to load its first code file from a network.

tldr.problem: Different computer makers used different methods to load startup code over a network. Supporting several kinds of machines could require several boot servers.
tldr.mechanism: The booting machine sends a TFTP read request for a named file and receives the file in TFTP data packets. RARP can supply the machine's Internet address when it does not know it.
tldr.outcome: The memo proposes TFTP for bootstrap loading and asks the ARPA Internet community for discussion. Its example boot code fits in less than 4K bytes, excluding the Ethernet driver.

facts.label: Example boot code
facts.value: Less than 4K bytes, excluding Ethernet driver

today: RFC 906 presents a proposed protocol for the ARPA Internet community and requests discussion. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Network Booting Needed a Common Method
sections.content:
Diskless workstations and other computers may load code files across a network when they start. The RFC says manufacturers had used different methods for this initial loading, so an installation with different machines might need several kinds of boot server. The machines could still communicate with one another after booting.

The memo proposes Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) as a common method. TFTP uses the Internet Protocol (IP) and is intended to be simple to implement. The RFC notes that its slower transfer is acceptable for the primary bootstrap; a later bootstrap can use a faster protocol. The proposal specifies network protocols, not how a user starts the machine or which data-link network it uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers used different ways to fetch startup files. RFC 906 proposes one shared method: ask for the file with TFTP, then use another method later if faster loading is needed.

sections.title: The Booting Machine's Network Request
sections.content:
The computer being started, called the booter, sends a TFTP read request (RRQ) containing the file name. It then receives TFTP DATA packets and sends ACK or ERROR packets as TFTP specifies. The file name should not depend on one operating system's naming rules. The booter does not need to answer incoming TFTP read or write requests.

TFTP runs over UDP over IP. The booter must accept IP datagrams of up to 524 octets, excluding the IP header: the RFC gives a maximum TFTP data packet of 516 octets and an 8-octet UDP header. If the booter knows its hardware address but not its Internet address, it may use RARP to learn the latter. If it knows a server's Internet address, it may use ARP to find that server's hardware address. The proposal also discusses sending the request to a broadcast address when the server is not known.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting computer asks for a file by name, then receives pieces and acknowledges them. If it does not know its own Internet address, it can ask RARP to find it from its hardware address.

sections.title: The Ethernet ROM Example
sections.content:
The RFC describes an implementation for a Motorola 68000 workstation that boots over Ethernet, with its startup code stored in ROM. A user supplies a file name and may also supply the workstation's Internet address and a server's Internet address. If the workstation address is missing, the code broadcasts a RARP request and stops booting if it times out. It uses ARP to look up a known server's Ethernet address; otherwise it uses broadcast addresses as described in the memo.

The boot code sends a TFTP read request and may hear from several servers. It does not stop after an error from one server, because another may send the requested data. The first valid data packet determines the addresses used for acknowledgements. The implementation uses less than 4K bytes of code, not counting the Ethernet device driver.
sections.plainLanguage: The example stores a small boot program in ROM. It finds network addresses when needed, asks for the file, and follows the first server that sends valid data.
